title: Meeting skills
description: Installs preparing-client-meetings, which turns pull requests and tracker tickets into what to say at dailies and weeklies, in a weekly note in the user's Obsidian vault, and writes a pull request scheduled for a later day into the first meeting after it opens. The vault is found on the local filesystem and the trackers are read through the MCP servers the project already has.

content: description: Prepares what to say at a daily standup or a weekly status meeting from pull requests and tracker tickets, plans the coming week's meetings and work, and writes a pull request scheduled with scheduling-pull-requests into the first meeting after it opens, all in a weekly note in the user's Obsidian vault. The update is a short, friendly paragraph written to be read aloud, saying what you finished and then your main focus, every sentence traceable to a pull request or ticket. Use when asked to prepare a daily, a standup, a weekly or a status meeting, to say what to report at a meeting, or to plan the week. Not for posting a Linear project update, which writing-linear-updates owns, or for writing anything to a tracker.

compatibility: Needs gh with read access to the repositories, python3, and the Obsidian vault on the local filesystem. Reads Jira through the atlassian MCP server and Linear through linear-server when the session has them; without one it reports from GitHub alone and says so.

A meeting update says what you finished since the last meeting and what your main focus is now, and raises a blocker only when there is one. **It is read aloud as written**, so it is a few short sentences of plain prose, not a list. **Every sentence traces to a pull request or a ticket**, or to a pull request scheduled to open before the meeting, and says what will be true when the meeting starts.

Plain Markdown in the user's Obsidian vault, the directory that contains `.obsidian/`. Find it before writing anything, and if there is none, say so and return the text. **Never write these files into a code repository.**
Meetings.md      the roster: one row per recurring meeting
2026-W40.md      one note per ISO week: the plan, then each meeting

No frontmatter, and a paragraph is one line, because Obsidian shows a single newline as a line break. Read a note before changing it, change only the section you own, and never reword what the user wrote.
`Meetings/Meetings.md` is one line saying what it is, then one table the user fills:
| Acme | daily | Mon–Fri 09:30–09:45 | acme/api, acme/web | Jira ACME |
- **Meeting** is `daily` or `weekly`; a client with both has two rows.
- **When** is local time with an end, so clashes can be seen.
Preparing a meeting works without a row; planning the week needs the rows. Never add a row or a value from a guess; one the user states may be written in.

1. **Identify the meeting.** The request says daily or weekly; a standup is a daily, a status meeting a weekly. With a roster row for it, use the row. Without one, use the repository in the current directory (`gh repo view --json nameWithOwner`) and whichever tracker the session can read. Ask only when there is neither a row nor a repository.

2. **Find the window**, from the previous occurrence of the meeting to now. With a row, that is the previous slot: Friday's for a daily on Monday. Without one, the same time on the previous working day for a daily, and seven days back for a weekly.
3. **Collect from GitHub** with this skill's script, given the repositories (`owner/*` becomes `--org owner`) and the tracker key when there is one:
python3 <this skill's directory>/scripts/collect.py --repo acme/api --repo acme/web --key ACME --since 2026-09-25T09:30

It prints your pull requests merged or closed without merging in the window, your open ones ready for review with who they wait on, your drafts, the reviews you gave, and pull requests waiting on your review. It changes nothing. Exit code 1 names a repository it could not read: say which, and go on.

4. **Read the tracker**, when there is one: your tickets whose status changed in the window, and blockers, meaning a ticket flagged, in a blocked status, or with an open "is blocked by" link. For Jira, through the `atlassian` MCP server: `assignee = currentUser() AND project = ACME AND updated >= "2026-09-25 09:30"`. For Linear, through `linear-server`. Without a row, read the tickets whose keys the pull requests carry. With no tracker, or without its tools in this session, write "Tracker not read" in the note and carry on from GitHub.
5. **Take the main focus from this week's plan**: its first items that are not done yet. With no plan, take the drafts and the tracker's in-progress tickets, and say so in the reply.

6. **Write the update** into this week's note under `## Mon 28 Sep — Acme daily`, creating the note if needed, and show it in the reply. Without a row, the repository name stands in for the client. Preparing the same meeting again replaces its section.

scheduling-pull-requests hands over a pull request that opens later: the repository, the branch, the opening time, the ticket key, and one plain sentence saying what changed. The work reads as done on the opening day, so it is reported at the first meeting after the opening time, and at no earlier one.
1. **Find the row** for the repository. Without one, write nothing and say so: there is no meeting to report it at.

2. **Find the meeting**: the first occurrence of that row after the opening time. For a Mon–Fri 09:30 daily and an opening on Friday at 17:12, that is Monday's daily. For a Thursday weekly, it is the next Thursday's.

3. **Write its section** in that meeting's ISO-week note, `## Mon 5 Oct — Acme daily` in `2026-W41.md`, creating the note if needed and keeping the meetings in the order they happen. If the section already exists, add the sentence to what its update says you finished, and leave the rest alone.

4. **Write one sentence** from the one handed over, as finished work that is ready for review, in the spoken style below: `Invoices can now be downloaded as a CSV file, and it's ready for review.` A daily and a weekly say it the same way.
5. **Write Sources** from what exists, since the pull request has no URL yet: `Sources: csv-export, pull request opening Fri 2 Oct 17:12; ACME-9`.

Write only that sentence and its Sources. The rest of the meeting is not known yet. Preparing the meeting as usual before it starts replaces the section, and by then the pull request is open and the collector finds it.
One paragraph of full sentences in the first person, with no bullets, bold labels, headings or symbols. Two parts, always in this order, so listeners know what is coming:
1. **What you finished.** Features and fixes merged or released since the last meeting, most visible first, then pull requests you opened that are ready for review, with who is reviewing them.
2. **Your main focus.** One sentence, "My main focus today is…" at a daily or "My main focus this week is…" at a weekly, naming one or two items.
Then, only when one exists, a blocker and who can clear it, and at a weekly a decision you need and from whom. Say each as a plain ask.
**Daily, under about fifty words**, roughly twenty seconds. **Weekly, under about a hundred and twenty words**, roughly a minute.

**Say what happened, never what did not.** No "nothing merged", "nothing's blocking me", "no progress on" or "still waiting". A part with nothing in it is left out without comment: with nothing merged, open with what is ready for review; with nothing ready either, open with the main focus.
Under the paragraph, `Sources:` links each pull request and ticket used. It is for checking, not for reading out. Link only URLs you read; a ticket the tracker did not return stays a plain key.
- **Done:** Invoices are no longer sent twice when a payment retries.
- **In review:** Invoice export as CSV, waiting on @dana.
Since Friday, invoices are no longer sent twice when a payment retries, and the CSV export is ready for review with Dana. My main focus today is moving the tax rules into one place.

- **Written for the ear.** Short sentences, one idea each, said the way you would say them across a table. Contractions are fine. Nothing that only works on a page: no brackets, slashes, "e.g.", "PR", or figures a listener has to hold.

- **Friendly but professional.** First person, plain verbs, a light link between parts such as "Since Friday" or "Next". No greeting, sign-off, filler or hype: not "hope everyone had a great weekend", not "super excited".
- **People by name.** Say the first name colleagues use, from the tracker or the GitHub profile, never an @handle. With nothing but a handle, say it without the @.

- **Plain words for any audience.** Say what someone who never saw the code would notice. Ticket keys, and schema, model, service or repository names, stay out of the spoken update; they belong in the Sources line and the plan.
- **Say the result, not the method.** "Invoices are no longer sent twice when a payment retries", not "add an idempotency key to the payment webhook".
- **One sentence per item**, about fifteen words. Several pull requests for one ticket are one item; two small items of the same kind may share a sentence.

- **Rephrase, never add.** Plainer words for what the source says, never an effect it does not state. "Customers can export invoices as CSV" rephrases `feat: export invoices as CSV`; "saves finance a day a month" adds.
- **Accuracy first, then the word budget.** To fit, drop a minor item rather than squeeze it in; never drop a blocker.
- **Merged is not released.** Say released only when a release after the merge exists, such as a merged release pull request or a tag.
- **Closed without merging never counts**, and a claim in its title, such as "twice as fast", goes with it.
- **A draft is in progress, not in review.**
- **No number nobody measured, and no impact no source states.**
- **A blocker names the thing and who can clear it.** "Might be blocked" is a risk, not a blocker, and stays out.
- **A quiet window stays short, not padded.** Leave out what did not happen rather than announce it, and never dress up in-progress work as finished to fill the gap.

- **Finished work is never presented as still in progress.** Work whose pull request is scheduled to open later is reported from the first meeting after it opens, as "A scheduled pull request" says. To spread work out, schedule its pull request with scheduling-pull-requests instead of saying it is not done.
At the weekend, or when asked to plan the week:

1. **Lay out next week's meetings by day** from the roster, and **name every clash**: two meetings whose times overlap. With an empty roster, say so: the plan covers the current repository's work only, and no clash can be checked.

2. **List the committed work per client**, in the tracker's own order: your tickets in the open sprint or cycle that are not done (Jira: `assignee = currentUser() AND project = ACME AND sprint in openSprints() AND statusCategory != Done ORDER BY Rank`), then your open pull requests on other tickets. Never set a priority or estimate a date. Without a tracker, the open pull requests are the list, and the plan says so.
3. **Write `## Plan`** directly under the first line of next week's note, creating the note if needed. If a plan exists, update it and keep what the user added.
The plan is a list of work, not a script. Each meeting's main focus is read from it, and what you finished comes from what actually happened since the last meeting.
The file is named after the ISO week, `2026-W40.md`. No heading at the top: the file name is the title.
| Thu 1 Oct | 09:30 Acme daily, 09:30 Globex weekly |
Clashes: Thu 1 Oct 09:30, Acme daily and Globex weekly.
- ACME-9 Invoice export as CSV (in review, api#39)
- ACME-10 Tax rules in one place (draft, api#41)
Open pull requests only: Globex has no tracker.
Since Friday, invoices are no longer sent twice when a payment retries, and the CSV export is ready for review with Dana. My main focus today is moving the tax rules into one place.
Dates are absolute. Meeting sections follow in the order the meetings happen.
- Every spoken sentence traces to an entry in its Sources line.
- The update is one paragraph read aloud as written: no bullets, labels or @handles, and within its word budget.
- It says what you finished, then "My main focus today" or "this week", and mentions nothing that did not happen.
- Nothing closed without merging is reported, and no draft is called in review.
- The tracker was read, or the note says it was not.
- No roster value, priority, date, number or impact was guessed.
- The spoken update is plain and friendly; keys and internal names appear only in Sources and the plan.
- The files are in the vault, not in a repository.
- A scheduled pull request appears only under the first meeting after it opens.

Prints six sections for the repositories or organisations given: pull requests
you merged in the window, ones you closed without merging in the window, your
open pull requests ready for review, your open drafts, reviews you gave on other
people's pull requests in the window, and open pull requests waiting on your
review. Lines are sorted by ticket key.
Reads GitHub through `gh api` and changes nothing.
WHEN is ISO 8601: 2026-09-25, 2026-09-25T09:30, or with an offset. A time
without an offset is local time. Open pull requests are shown as they are now,
even when --until is in the past.
Exit codes: 0 on success; 1 when a repository or organisation could not be
read, with everything else still printed; 2 on a usage or gh error.
